newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam plans to prevent unemployment crisis.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam plans to prevent unemployment crisis.

text.p: Vietnam plans to create millions of jobs between now and the end of the century to prevent the country's ranks of unemployed swelling to crisis levels, the state-run daily Vietnam News said on Friday.
"According to unofficial statistics, Vietnam has a higher rate of unemployment than any other country in Asia," the paper said.
"These figures claim that an estimated six or seven percent of Vietnam's working-age population are either jobless or under-employed," it said.
It said authorities hoped to create 3.7 million permanent jobs for the unemployed and under-employed and provide training for at least five million workers.
It gave no details of the job creation schemes being planned.
An official at the Ministry of Planning and Investment said earlier this year that, based on current trends, the number of people without work would climb to 8.5 million by 2000.
According to a Labour Ministry estimate, the figure now stands at 2.4 million, or seven percent of the working population.
"Unemployment, already a problem in Vietnam, is in danger of getting worse as another 1.2 million people reach working age each year," Vietnam News said.
"Most of these youngsters are in rural areas, where 75 percent of the country's labour force is concentrated."
It said that with the population, currently around 75 million, growing at an annual rate of 1.5-1.8 percent and rural areas giving way to urbanisation, the country faced the prospect of overcrowding.

Since farming is seasonal, most rural workers are without work for 30-35 percent of the year. Handicraft production remains undeveloped in most villages and so many farmers migrate to cities or towns in search of casual work.
Vietnam News said restructuring of the country's sprawling state sector had left 50,000 workers redundant and 15 percent of its workforce under-employed.
"At many state enterprises employees work only three or four days a week," it said.
